title: A Classroom Investigation
paragraphs: A class was investigating how writers turn observations into evidence. The teacher supplied a folder of short accounts and asked the students to look beyond their first impressions. Each account described a particular situation, but the collection raised questions that could apply more widely.

Several records provided a starting point for the discussion. The two arrows point in opposite directions. We have only a partial account because several pages are missing. Our primary concern is safety; everything else is less important. The remote campsite was far from roads and houses.

Other records complicated that first impression and encouraged a closer reading. After the meeting, the teachers returned to their respective classrooms. Each snowflake has a unique pattern unlike any other in the collection. The rule has universal application: it applies to everyone in the group. The fence marks the boundary between the two farms.

The class finished by comparing its first impressions with its later interpretations. Some ideas had survived closer examination; others needed to be revised. The students kept the original details visible so that future readers could judge for themselves. They understood that a convincing explanation should connect the evidence clearly while leaving room for questions the records could not answer.

targets.definition: completely different or facing the other way
incomplete or covering only some of the whole
of first importance or occurring first
far from populated places or usual routes
belonging separately to each of several people
the only one of its kind
a line marking a limit or edge
